The respondent was a member of the service of the respondent. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been dismissed from service. He was reinstated in service with a further punishment of dismissal. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Chief Settlement Commissioner and the Tribunal. The High Court allowed the petition and quashed the order of dismissal. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Tribunal had power to modify the penalty, and (ii) the punishment of dismissal awarded to the respondent was reduced to that of stoppage of his five increments which he had earned for a period of five years in terms of clause (iv) of Rule 11 of the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965. The trial court held that the will was of sound and disposing state of mind and restored the order of the primary judge. The High Court held that the appellant had failed to prove the due and valid execution of the will. The High court held that on the proof of the signature of the deceased or his signature the appellant had made a material alteration of the evidence. The High. Court held that on a proper construction of the will the appellant had not proved the due and proper execution of the Will. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the appellant was not in a sound and disposing State of India. The appellant came into the family of the testator and was in possession. The petitioners in these petitions have challenged the validity of a notification issued by the Government of Gujarat on June 26, 1985 in exercise of its powers conferred by section 15 of the (67 of 1957) read with section 15 of that Act, by which the State of Gujarat was empowered to levy royalty in respect of minor minerals. The respondents claimed that the amounts were not income of the Hindu undivided family but merely represented inheritance or realisations of the assets of the family. The respondents contended that the amounts in question were not income from the family and that the amounts should be deemed to be income of the family and not the income of the deceased. The Income tax Officer held that the amounts could not be taxed as income. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the notice under section 34 could validly be served only for the assessment years 1950 51 and 1952 53. The High Court in appeal held that the notices under section 34 were not liable to be issued on the death of the deceased and that the notices were invalid. The High court held that the proceedings under section 34 had no application to the case. The High. Court held that the assessment could not be made on the death or not and that section 24B had no application. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the notice was not a valid notice. The question whether a particular amount was income or not had nothing to do with the time of its receipt and the question of receipt was material only for the purpose of determining whether on that amount tax was to be levied under the Act in the year of assessment. The assessee was keeping accounts on cash basis and he was entitled to assess the total income of the assessee as if the legal representatives were the assessees. The assessee 's case was that the amounts which were sought to be taxed and which had been held not to be liable to tax were those which were not received in the previous year and were therefore not liable to tax. [719 H; 819 A]
